Sat, Oct 10th @ 11:00 PM|Elapsed: 1:57Correct

The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point.

If F represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field F=Pi+Qj with a simply connected domain D⊆R2 has a stream function ψ(x,y) if and only if ∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=0.

Note that F(x,y)=2xi−2yj is a vector field with simply connected domain D, where P(x,y)=2x and Q(x,y)=−2y. Computing the partial derivatives, we have

∂P∂x=2,∂Q∂y=−2.

Hence, F has a stream function, since

∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=2−2=0.

Next, we find a stream function. A function ψ(x,y) is a stream function of the vector field F=Pi+Qj if

P=∂ψ∂y,Q=−∂ψ∂x.

In our case, we have ∂ψ∂y=2x,∂ψ∂x=2y.

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

ψ(x,y)=2xy+f(x),ψ(x,y)=2xy+g(y)

where f and g are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting f=g=0, we have

ψ(x,y)=2xy.

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function ψ(x,y)=2xy given by the equations ψ(x,y)=c.

Notice that the range of ψ(x,y) is (−∞,∞). So, we will consider level curves for any value of c. So, we have:

ψ(x,y)=c2xy=cy=cx

Sat, Oct 10th @ 11:20 PM|Elapsed: 0:01Incorrect

Recall that if xh(t) satisfies a homogeneous linear system x′(t)=Ax(t) and xp(t) is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t), then xh(t)+xp(t) is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the linearity principle for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if x1(t), x2(t),…,xk(t) are solutions to a homogeneous linear system x′(t)=Ax(t), then any linear combination c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)+⋯+ckxk(t) with c1,c2,…,ck∈R is also a solution of the same homogeneous system.

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

  • Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination xh(t)=2⋅x1(t) is a solution to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t) according to the linearity principle. Thus, 2⋅x1(t)⏟xh(t)+xp(t) is a solution to our inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).

  • Option II might be not a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that x1(t)−x2(t) can't be written as xh(t)+xp(t), where xh(t) is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term xp(t).

  • Option III might be not a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that 3⋅xp(t) can't be written as xh(t)+xp(t), where xh(t) is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier 3 next to the particular solution xp(t).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

Sat, Oct 10th @ 11:20 PM|Elapsed: 0:01Incorrect

A numerical method yn+1=yn+Δyn is stable for a given step size Δx if, when applied to the test equation y′=−λy,y(0)=1,x≥0,λ>0, the numerical solution satisfies yn→0 as n→∞, just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form yn+1=R(λΔx)yn, where R(λΔx) is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by |R(λΔx)|<1, is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the implicit Euler method is R(λΔx)=11+λΔx.

Let's check the stability of the implicit Euler Method for each of the given values in turn.

  • For λΔx=0.1, we have |R(0.1)|=|11+0.1|=|11.1|=0.9090…<1.✓ Since this value falls within the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

  • For λΔx=0.8, we have |R(0.8)|=|11+0.8|=|11.8|=0.5555…<1.✓ Since this value falls within the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

  • For λΔx=1.2, we have |R(1.2)|=|11+1.2|=|12.2|=0.4545…<1.✓ Since this value falls within the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

  • For λΔx=5, we have |R(5)|=|11+5|=|16|=0.1666…<1.✓ Since this value falls within the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, III, and IV".

Note that, since the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable, it is stable for all possible values of λΔx.

53.Identifying True Statements Regarding the Spectral Theorem?

Given that A is a real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

  2. A is not diagonalizable
  3. If u and v are two eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues, then u⊥v

Sun, Oct 11th @ 3:54 AM|Elapsed: 0:07Incorrect

Given that A is an n×n symmetric matrix over R, the spectral theorem states the following:

  • The eigenvalues of A are all real.

  • Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

  • The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

  • A is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. According to the spectral theorem, the eigenvalues are real.

  • Statement II is false. According to the spectral theorem, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable, so, A is diagonalizable.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

73.Calculating the Z-Score of a Given Observation?

Sun, Oct 11th @ 4:33 AM|Elapsed: 0:51Correct

z=x−x―σ.

The z-score represents how many standard deviations an observation is above or below the data set's mean.

Here, we're told that the mean is x―=17, and we can calculate the standard deviation as

σ=σ2=4.06.

So, the z-score of the observation x=12.3 is given by
